newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti's Caio faces new probe.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti's Caio faces new probe.

text.p: The stock of crisis-hit Olivetti slumped Monday as its chief executive, Francesco Caio, faced grilling by magistrates on the company's finances.

Caio, who has headed the making-losing information technology group for just over 10 turbulent weeks, will be questioned in a preliminary probe of the group's accounts by magistrates Olivetti's home town of Ivrea near Turin, judicial sources said.

The questioning is the first step of an investigation that could lead to a full-scale criminal inquiry into statements made by the struggling group on its financial accounts and follows a similar probe by stock market watchdog authority Consob.

The move unnerved Olivetti shares, which fell to a record low of 515 lire before being automatically suspended by the Milan bourse for falling the 10 percent limit. After a failed attempt to restart trading, the shares remained suspended.

Ivrea magistrates, who launched their inquiry over the weekend, have questioned former Olivetti director-general in charge of finance and auditing, Renzo Francesconi, after he cast doubts on the accuracy of the group's first-half accounts.

Olivetti's stock began to slide earlier in the day after the group cancelled anxiously awaited analysts' meetings this week and delayed the publication of its fully detailed first-half 1996 results until the end of this month.

Late on Friday, Olivetti called off the analysts meetings, scheduled in Milan on Monday and in London on Tuesday, as the crisis-hit group attempted to satisfy an earlier investigation by stock market watchdog Consob over its financial accounts.

Earlier this month, Olivetti reported initial first-half 1996 results showing sales sliding, losses continuing and debts deepening. Francesconi resigned a day later after he questioned the validity of the group's financial figures.

Financial analysts said the group must produce a full set of approved accounts before the process of re-building confidence can start. Market talk that the group's debts were worse than reported had already prompted selling of the shares.
Olivetti has recorded losses for the last five years and seems set to make it six years after reporting a 440.2 billion lire ($290 million) loss in the first six months of 1996.

Its new businesss of mobile and fixed line telephone networks continue to absorb cash while its older core business of personal computers, office equipment and computer systems falter under stiff competitive pressures.

Foreign funds invested heavily in Olivetti as part of a rights issue a year ago and these overseas shareholders, holding 70 percent of Olivetti, have been demanding more financial information from the group.
